title: Why taste with a method
subtitle: Drinking versus tasting
objectives: Explain why a method helps you taste
Name the three steps of tasting
Set up good conditions for tasting

steps.title: Tasting is paying attention
steps.body: Drinking is enjoying. Tasting is noticing what you're enjoying, in an order that lets you compare. The method is simple: look, smell, taste. Doing it the same way each time builds a memory of wines you can draw on later.

steps.title: Why the order matters
steps.body: Each step prepares the next. The look hints at age and body. The nose works before the palate because most of what we call flavour is smell: the tongue senses only sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. When you sip, aromas travel up the back of the throat to the nose, a route called retronasal smell.

steps.prompt: Why do you smell a wine before you taste it?
options: Most of what we call flavour is smell
steps.explanation: The tongue registers five basic tastes. Everything else, from cherry to vanilla, is detected by smell, before and during the sip.

steps.body: Taste in daylight or under white light, against a white background, with a clean, plain glass. Avoid perfume, coffee and toothpaste just before. Small changes like these make a bigger difference than expensive gear.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of tasting in order.
steps.explanation: Swirling releases aromas between looking and smelling. The conclusion comes once you've taken everything in.

steps.title: What you learned
points: A method turns drinking into tasting you can compare
Most flavour is smell, so the nose comes before the palate
White light, a plain glass and no strong smells help
